dek.text: Texas A&M plans an automated lab where robots mix, melt and test new alloys. A separate NSF platform is funded for six years and open to outside researchers.

introduction.text: [A {{money:c1}} grant is going to Texas A&M's Department of Materials Science and Engineering](c1). [It comes from the WoodNext Foundation and will help researchers build a campus facility](c2) [meant to use robotics and artificial intelligence to speed up the development of new alloys](c3). [The foundation's support will create what the university calls the Aggie AI Foundry](c5).

[Robots are to mix, melt and test the materials with computer controlled arms along an assembly line that takes samples](c8). [The university says existing self driving labs can't handle new metal alloys at temperatures up to {{number:c10}} degrees Celsius](c10). [Those labs focus on materials that are relatively easy to make](c11).

sections.heading: Why software alone does not settle it

paragraphs.text: [Several dozen elements from the periodic table give AI roughly a trillion possible ways to mix them](c18). [Raymundo Arróyave says no computational tool anywhere in the world can predict how an alloy is going to behave](c17). That is the reason the plan ends in a furnace and a test rather than in a prediction.

[Arróyave leads PhaseForge](c29), [free open software paid for by a National Science Foundation award that uses machine learning](c30). [It applies machine learning to CALPHAD, a method that is decades old](c32), [and tells researchers whether a material they want to build can exist at all](c33). [It is distributed free online and anyone may contribute to it](c31).

sections.heading: Who conceived it and who is paying

paragraphs.text: [Ibrahim Karaman, who heads the department](c14), [is one of the two researchers who conceived the foundry](c13). [Arróyave is the other](c15). [The two have published more than {{number:c16}} papers together](c16). [The university calls the foundry the first lab of its kind in academia, and that claim is its own](c12).

[The WoodNext Foundation manages the philanthropy of the founder and chief executive of Roku](c4), [Anthony Wood, and his wife Susan](c5). [The money flows through a donor advised fund program called the WoodNext TAMU Fund](c6).

[The National Science Foundation has a platform of its own at Texas A&M, the Autonomous Robotic Metallurgist](c20). [Its award record names the Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station as recipient](c24) [and lists {{number:c25}} dollars obligated](c25) [of an estimated total of {{number:c26}} dollars](c26). [The award runs from {{date:c27}}](c27) [to {{date:c28}}](c28).

[NSF describes the platform as an open access facility](c21), [built to design, make, test and learn from new alloys](c22). [Its intended users include researchers at non-R1 and EPSCoR institutions](c23).

sections.heading: What is a goal and what is a result

paragraphs.text: [Texas A&M says the automated process will cut alloy development from months to a week or less, which is a stated goal and not a measured result](c9). No source checked for this story gives an opening date for the foundry or a construction timeline. The NSF award record gives its own dates, and those belong to the federal platform rather than to the WoodNext facility.
